Part A

Agility and the Agile Manifesto

0:00–0:14

Goal of the lesson. Define agility; state the four values of the Agile Manifesto and group its twelve principles; compare agile and plan-driven development; use the five factors of Boehm and Turner to decide how agile a project can be.

Today's question

Good morning. Last Tuesday each team chose a process model for its product and began a decision record, and several of you used the word agile for working in short increments. Today we give the word a precise meaning, in four questions. What does a team commit to when it says it is agile? How does Scrum organise that commitment? Which practices of Extreme Programming and Kanban make short cycles possible, and how does a team plan them with numbers? And how does an organisation improve its process, with models such as CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration)?

This is the second hour on LO1 (Learning Outcome 1): by the end of it you should be able to argue for and against the agile methods and the process-improvement standards, as the Final will ask you to do. There is no new Block today; the Studio is coached time to finish Block 3.

Agility

Start with the word itself.

agility — The ability of a software team to respond to change — in the requirements, the technology, the team or the priorities — quickly and at low cost, while it continues to deliver working software.

Your textbook, Pressman and Maxim, 9th edition, chapter 3↗scan, adds three conditions: the team communicates with everyone who has a stake in the product, brings the customer into the team, and organises itself so that it controls its own work.

agile software development — A family of methods — Scrum, XP (Extreme Programming), Kanban and others — that build software in short iterations, deliver a working increment frequently, and use the feedback on each increment to decide what to build next.

Why would a team want this? Because requirements change while a product is being built: users discover what they need when they see the first version. In a process that freezes the requirements at the start, every later change means rework. Agile methods treat change as normal and organise the work so that a change costs as little as possible: small batches of work, frequent tests, frequent feedback.

On the slide 5: What agility means
What agility means
  • Agility: respond to change quickly and at low cost, while still delivering working software
  • Three conditions: talk with every stakeholder · bring the customer into the team · the team controls its own work
  • Agile software development: short iterations, a working increment often, feedback decides the next step
  • Why: users discover what they need when they see a first version
Plan once, then buildA change discovered late means rework of finished documents, design and code.
Build in short cyclesA change discovered late is the input of the next iteration.

The Agile Manifesto

In February 2001, seventeen practitioners met at Snowbird, in Utah. Each of them had created or used a lightweight method, such as Scrum, Extreme Programming, Crystal or Feature-Driven Development. They disagreed on many details, but they agreed on one short text, the Manifesto for Agile Software Development↗scan, usually called the Agile Manifesto, with twelve principles↗scan behind it. Jim Highsmith, one of them, tells the story on the history page↗scan.

The Manifesto is not a method. It does not say how long an iteration lasts or who does what. It states values: what its authors valued more when two good things conflicted.

On the slide 6: The Agile Manifesto (2001)
The Agile Manifesto (2001)
  • February 2001, Snowbird, Utah: seventeen practitioners
  • They came from Scrum, XP (Extreme Programming), Crystal, Feature-Driven Development and other lightweight methods
  • They agreed on four values and twelve principles
  • A statement of priorities, not a method: no iteration length, no roles
2001Snowbird, Utah
17signatories
4values
12principles

The four values

The Manifesto has four values, each written as a comparison of two items:

  1. individuals and interactions over processes and tools;
  2. working software over comprehensive documentation;
  3. customer collaboration over contract negotiation;
  4. responding to change over following a plan.

Read the sentence that follows them with care: the authors write that the items on the right still have value, but that they value the items on the left more. The Manifesto does not reject processes, tools, documentation, contracts or plans. It sets priorities for the moment when two of them conflict.

The most common misunderstanding starts here. “We are agile, so we write no documentation” is false. An agile team writes the documentation it needs, at the time it needs it, and keeps it short enough to stay correct. The documents in your repository — the charter, the decision record, next week's requirements — are exactly that: short, current, and useful to the next person who reads them.

On the slide 7: The four values
The four values
  • The items on the left are valued more
  • The items on the right still have value
  • “We are agile, so we write no documentation” is a misreading
  • Agile documentation: the documents the team needs, when it needs them, short enough to stay correct
individuals and interactionsoverprocesses and tools
working softwareovercomprehensive documentation
customer collaborationovercontract negotiation
responding to changeoverfollowing a plan

The twelve principles

The twelve principles turn the values into rules for daily work. Here they are in my words, in four groups; the official page↗scan gives the original wording.

  • The customer and value (principles 1–3): satisfy the customer by delivering valuable software early and continuously; welcome changing requirements, even late in the project; deliver working software frequently, from a couple of weeks to a couple of months, with a preference for the shorter timescale.
  • People (principles 4–6): business people and developers work together every day; build projects around motivated people, with the support and the trust they need; inside a team, face-to-face conversation is the most effective way to pass on information.
  • Progress and pace (principles 7–8): working software is the primary measure of progress; development is sustainable, so that sponsors, developers and users can keep a constant pace indefinitely.
  • Quality and reflection (principles 9–12): constant attention to technical excellence and good design; simplicity, which means not doing work that is not needed; the best architectures, requirements and designs come from teams that organise themselves; at regular intervals the team reflects on how to become more effective and adjusts its behaviour.

Two of them return later today: working software as the measure of progress in Lesson 4, and regular reflection in Lesson 5.

On the slide 8: The twelve principles, in four groups
The twelve principles, in four groups
  • Customer and value (1–3): early, continuous delivery · welcome change · frequent delivery, the shorter timescale preferred
  • People (4–6): business and developers together daily · motivated, trusted people · face-to-face conversation
  • Progress and pace (7–8): working software measures progress · sustainable development, a constant pace
  • Quality and reflection (9–12): technical excellence · simplicity · self-organising teams · regular reflection

Agile and plan-driven development

plan-driven development — Development in which the requirements, the design and the schedule are planned in detail at the start, and progress is measured against that plan; the Waterfall and V-models of last week are its classic forms.

The table compares the two on seven points.

Neither is better in general. A plan-driven process is the right choice when the requirements are stable and must be approved in advance — a payroll module bound by law, or a medical device that a regulator certifies. An agile process is the right choice when the requirements will change because the users learn what they need by using the product — most web and mobile applications, including the five products of this course.

On the slide 9: Agile versus plan-driven
Agile versus plan-driven
AgilePlan-driven
Requirementsemerge and change during the projectfixed and approved early
Planningre-planned at every iterationdetailed plan at the start
Deliverya working increment every few weeksone release, or a few, at the end
Documentationjust enough, written when neededcomprehensive, written before the code
Customerworks with the team continuouslyreviews at milestones
Progress measured byworking softwarecompleted phases and documents
A change isexpected inputhandled by a formal change request

When agile fits — the five factors

How do you decide for a real project? Barry Boehm and Richard Turner published an answer in 2003 (Computer, 36(6)↗scan); Boehm is also the author of COCOMO (Constructive Cost Model), which you used last week. They describe a project by five factors:

  • size — how many people work on the product;
  • criticality — the worst loss a defect could cause: from a loss of comfort, through a loss of money, to one human life or many;
  • dynamism — how much of the requirements changes each month;
  • personnel — how many people need a written procedure, and how many can adapt a method. Boehm and Turner use Alistair Cockburn's skill levels: Level 1B people can follow a procedure, Level 2 and 3 people can adapt or even rewrite a method, and Level 1A lies between. Each tick of this axis gives two shares, Level 1B and Levels 2–3: 0 % and 35 % at the centre, 40 % and 15 % at the edge;
  • culture — whether the people prefer frequent change or fixed rules.

They draw the five factors as the axes of one polar chart. Near the centre lies the agile home ground: few people, low criticality, many changes, experienced people, a culture that likes change. Near the edge lies the plan-driven home ground: the opposite on all five axes.

On the slide 10: When agile fits (1/2): five factors
When agile fits (1/2): five factors
  • Boehm and Turner (2003): describe a project by five factors
  • Size — how many people · Criticality — worst loss a defect could cause
  • Dynamism — share of the requirements that change each month
  • Personnel — who can adapt a method, who needs a procedure
  • Culture — preference for frequent change or for fixed rules
  • Centre of their chart: agile home ground · edge: plan-driven home ground

Hybrids — and a Canadian example

Most real projects lie in neither home ground. Boehm and Turner's advice is a hybrid: use the agile method where the factors allow it, and add plan-driven discipline exactly where a factor pulls the project outward. A large team needs written interfaces between sub-teams; a critical system needs formal reviews and traceable tests; a team with many beginners needs written procedures. The rest of the work can stay agile.

Agile methods are not used only by start-ups. One of the Government of Canada Digital Standards↗scan, Iterate and improve frequently, asks federal teams to “develop services using agile, iterative and user-centred methods”, and the same teams keep the controls the law requires: budgets, approvals, audits. That is a hybrid in Boehm and Turner's sense.

After class, the module shows one team applying the five factors to its product. Now, three statements to test the values.

On the slide 11: When agile fits (2/2): most projects are hybrids
When agile fits (2/2): most projects are hybrids
  • Most projects sit between the two home grounds
  • Hybrid: agile where the factors allow it, written discipline where a factor pulls outward
  • SafeCampus: personnel 4, criticality 3, culture 3 → reviews, a Definition of Done, extra checks on incident data
  • Government of Canada Digital Standards: “Iterate and improve frequently” — with the controls the law requires

🏫Real-life example — SafeCampus: how agile can Team Heron be?

Task. Team Heron (fictional) builds SafeCampus: a student reports a hazard or an incident, optionally anonymously, and follows its status. Before writing its first user story, the team rates the product on Boehm and Turner's five factors, places the profile on their polar chart, and decides which parts of the work can run in short agile iterations and which need written, plan-driven discipline.
Relation to the lecture. It applies the question of Lesson 1 — when does agile fit? — with the five factors, and produces the verdict that a team writes in its process decision record.

The team argues each rating in one sentence. Size: four students, the first tick of the axis (3 people) — position 1. Dynamism: the campus security office has not yet decided which hazard categories it wants, so about 30 % of the requirements will change each month — position 2. Personnel: the team expects about 30 % of its work to be done at Level 1B, by members who still need a written procedure, and only about 20 % at Levels 2–3, by a member able to adapt the method; these are the two percentages of position 4, so the team wants written procedures for reviews and releases. Culture: half of the team likes to improvise, half wants rules — position 3. Criticality: SafeCampus is not an emergency line (emergencies go to the campus security telephone), so no life depends on it; but a lost or late report could delay the repair of a hazard and cause serious costs for the campus. On Boehm and Turner's scale (comfort, discretionary funds, essential funds, a single life, many lives), that is “essential funds”: position 3.

The profile touches the agile home ground on size and dynamism and moves outward on personnel, culture and criticality. The verdict is a hybrid: two-week iterations shown to the security office, plus three written pieces of discipline — a Definition of Done that every teammate follows, a review of every change by a second person, and extra tests on how incident reports are stored and delivered.

Execution steps — click one to go back to it
    Variables after this step
    Output
    Step-by-step explanation
    1. The first lines store the product name, the five factor names in chart order, and an empty dictionary ticks. Keeping the names in one list means every later loop visits the axes in the same order as the chart.
    2. Five lines fill ticks: for each axis, the five labels from the centre (agile) to the edge (plan-driven), with the values published by Boehm and Turner — for example 3, 10, 30, 100 and 300 people on the size axis.
    3. rating holds the team's five decisions as tick positions from 1 to 5. These are the only numbers a team chooses; everything else follows from them.
    4. The for loop visits the factors. For each one it reads the position, converts it to a list index (position − 1, because Python counts from 0) to fetch the label, and classifies the position: 1–2 agile, 3 between, 4–5 plan-driven. Watch the polygon in the visualisation gain one corner per iteration.
    5. The if position >= 3 test adds every factor that is not in the agile home ground to outward. For SafeCampus that list ends as personnel, culture and criticality.
    6. After the loop, the if / elif / else chooses the verdict: an empty list means agile; all five positions at 4 or 5 means plan-driven; any other mix is a hybrid, and the verdict names the outward factors.
    7. The last line prints the verdict. Pause there and compare it with the chart: the rust corners of the polygon are exactly the factors that need written discipline.
    Run it on your own computer too: python3 demo1_safecampus_agility_profile.py (Legal Notice, section 10: run code only on equipment you own or are allowed to use).

    Q1.1
    Multiple-choice question
    Which statement matches the value “working software over comprehensive documentation”? (one right answer)
    • ✘ Wrong — No. The Manifesto says the items on the right still have value; documentation is written when it is needed.
    • ✔ Right — Yes. The value sets a priority for conflicts; it does not remove documentation.
    • ✘ Wrong — No. Nothing in the Manifesto delays documentation to the end; agile teams write it when it is useful.
    • ✘ Wrong — No. The Manifesto contains no rule about contracts or forbidden documents.
    Hint: Read the sentence that follows the four values: what does it say about the items on the right?
    Q1.2
    Multiple-choice question
    About 50 % of a product's requirements change every month, and its team prefers frequent change. On Boehm and Turner's chart, these two factors point toward… (one right answer)
    • ✔ Right — Yes. High dynamism and a culture that likes change both lie at the centre of the chart.
    • ✘ Wrong — No. The plan-driven home ground has stable requirements (about 1 % change per month) and a culture that prefers order.
    • ✘ Wrong — No. Dynamism is one of the five factors: size, criticality, dynamism, personnel, culture.
    • ✘ Wrong — No. The edge is the plan-driven home ground; change is handled there by formal change requests.
    Hint: Is high dynamism near the centre or near the edge of the chart?
    Q1.3
    Multiple-choice question
    Which project is the clearest case for a plan-driven process? (one right answer)
    • ✘ Wrong — No. Requirements discovered by using a prototype call for an iterative, agile approach.
    • ✔ Right — Yes. Stable, legally fixed requirements approved in advance are the plan-driven home ground.
    • ✘ Wrong — No. Frequent change driven by feedback is the agile home ground.
    • ✘ Wrong — No. A small team with changing needs sits near the centre of the chart.
    Hint: Look for requirements that are stable and must be approved before coding.
    Q1.4
    Multiple-choice question
    In the SafeCampus example, which factor did Team Heron rate at position 4, pulling the product toward the plan-driven home ground? (one right answer)
    • ✘ Wrong — No. Four students sit at the first tick (3 people): position 1.
    • ✘ Wrong — No. About 30 % change per month: position 2, inside the agile home ground.
    • ✔ Right — Yes. About 30 % of the work at Level 1B and only 20 % at Levels 2–3 are the values of position 4: the team wants written procedures.
    • ✘ Wrong — No. “Essential funds” is position 3, between the two home grounds.
    Hint: Two ratings were inside the agile home ground and two were in the middle; one went further out.
    Q1.5
    Multiple-select question — choose every right answer
    Which statements about the Agile Manifesto are true? (2 right answers)
    • ✔ Right — True: Snowbird, Utah, February 2001, seventeen signatories.
    • ✔ Right — True: the values are on the home page, the principles on a second page.
    • ✘ Wrong — False: it asks for frequent delivery, from a couple of weeks to a couple of months, with a preference for the shorter timescale; it fixes no exact length.
    • ✘ Wrong — False: it is a statement by practitioners, not a standard of any standards body.
    • ✘ Wrong — False: contract negotiation still has value; customer collaboration is valued more.
    • ✘ Wrong — False: the Scrum Master is defined in the Scrum Guide, not in the Manifesto.
    Hint: Think about where and when it was written, and what it contains — not about method details.

    • ✔ Right — Correct: this is the discipline the personnel rating asks for.
    • ✔ Right — Correct: this answers the criticality rating.
    • ✘ Wrong — Wrong: that is the plan-driven extreme, and dynamism is at position 2.
    • ✘ Wrong — Wrong: a misreading of the second value.
    • ✘ Wrong — Wrong: position 3 already pulls outward and needs attention.

    Agile or not? Three statements
    0:10–0:14 · 4 minutes

    1. “We are agile, so we do not write documentation.”
    2. “Every two weeks we show the working product to the cafeteria manager and change the plan with what we learn.”
    3. “All the requirements are signed in September; any change needs a committee's approval.”
    Statement 1 — not agile: a misreading of the second value; documentation still has value. Statement 2 — agile: frequent delivery, customer collaboration, responding to change. Statement 3 — plan-driven; not wrong in itself: for a payroll module bound by law it can be the right choice.
    Part B
    Scrum
    0:14–0:26
    Goal of the lesson. Name the three accountabilities, the five events with their timeboxes and the three artifacts with their commitments; explain why only Done work counts; follow one Sprint from planning to retrospective.
    What Scrum is
    

    Scrum — A lightweight framework in which one small team delivers value in fixed-length iterations called Sprints, and inspects and adapts its progress every day, and the product and its way of working at the end of each Sprint.
    

    

    Scrum is defined by the Scrum Guide↗scan, written by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland. Its current official edition dates from November 2020 and is published under a CC BY-SA (Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licence). In 2025 Jeff Sutherland, John Coleman and Ralph Jocham published a companion, the Scrum Guide Expansion Pack↗scan; it adds guidance but does not replace the 2020 Guide, which remains the reference in this course.
    

    Scrum rests on empiricism: knowledge comes from experience, and decisions are made on what is observed. Three pillars make that possible:
    

      

    • transparency — the work and the process are visible to the people who do the work and to the people who receive it;
      • 

    • inspection — the artifacts and the progress toward the goals are checked frequently;
      • 

    • adaptation — when an inspection shows that something is outside acceptable limits, the team adjusts it as soon as possible.
      • 

    

    Scrum is short on purpose: three accountabilities, five events, three artifacts. Everything else — how to write stories, how to test, how to estimate — the team chooses.
    On the slide 15: Scrum: a framework built on empiricism
    Scrum: a framework built on empiricism
    • Scrum: one small team, fixed-length Sprints, inspect and adapt every day and at the end of each Sprint
    • Defined by the Scrum Guide (Schwaber and Sutherland), official edition of November 2020
    • 2025 Expansion Pack: a companion, not a replacement
    • Empiricism: decide on what is observed
    • Three pillars: transparency · inspection · adaptation
    • Deliberately short: 3 accountabilities · 5 events · 3 artifacts
    3accountabilities
    5events
    3artifacts
    3pillars
    The Scrum Team
    The Scrum Team is small — the Guide says typically ten people or fewer — with no sub-teams and no hierarchy. It holds three accountabilities. The Guide writes accountabilities rather than roles on purpose: what matters is who answers for which result.
    

    

    Product Owner — The person accountable for maximising the value of the product: develops and communicates the Product Goal, creates and orders the Product Backlog items, and keeps the backlog visible and understood. One person, not a committee.
    

    Scrum Master — The person accountable for the team's effectiveness and for establishing Scrum as the Guide defines it: coaches the team, causes impediments to be removed, and makes sure the events take place, are useful and stay within their timebox.
    

    Developers — The people who create a usable Increment every Sprint: they plan the Sprint, build quality in by following the Definition of Done, and adapt their plan every day toward the Sprint Goal.
    

    

    In a team of four students, one of you can be the Product Owner — the person who speaks with your client — another the Scrum Master, and all four are Developers. The rotating roles of your team charter — Coordinator, Scribe, Builder, Tester — can stay; Scrum adds who answers for the value of the product and who answers for the way you work.
    On the slide 16: The Scrum Team: three accountabilities
    The Scrum Team: three accountabilities
    • One small team, typically ten people or fewer, no sub-teams, no hierarchy
    • Product Owner — maximises the value of the product; orders the Product Backlog; one person
    • Scrum Master — the team's effectiveness; coaches; causes impediments to be removed; keeps the events in their timebox
    • Developers — create a usable Increment every Sprint; plan the Sprint; follow the Definition of Done
    • Your team of four: one Product Owner, one Scrum Master, four Developers
    Product Ownervalue of the product · Product Backlog
    Scrum Mastereffectiveness · impediments · events
    Developersthe Increment · the plan · quality
    The five events
    Scrum gives every event a timebox — a maximum duration that the event may not exceed. For a one-month Sprint the Guide sets the maxima in this table; for shorter Sprints, it says, the events are usually shorter.
    

    

    Sprint — The container of all the other events: a fixed period of one month or less in which the team turns ideas into a usable Increment. A new Sprint starts as soon as the previous one ends.
    

    

    Sprint Planning answers three questions: why is this Sprint valuable, what can be Done in this Sprint, and how will the chosen work get done; the answer to the first question becomes the Sprint Goal. The Daily Scrum takes 15 minutes, at the same time and place every working day: the Developers inspect their progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the plan. At the Sprint Review, the team and its stakeholders inspect what was built and decide what to do next; the Product Backlog may change. At the Sprint Retrospective, the team inspects how it worked — people, interactions, process, tools, its Definition of Done — and chooses the most useful improvements.
    On the slide 17: The five events and their timeboxes
    The five events and their timeboxes
    EventPurposeMaximum for a one-month Sprint
    Sprintcontainer of the other events: produce a usable Incrementone month
    Sprint Planningwhy, what and how of this Sprint; write the Sprint Goal8 hours
    Daily Scruminspect progress toward the Sprint Goal; adapt the plan15 minutes
    Sprint Reviewinspect the outcome with stakeholders; adapt the Product Backlog4 hours
    Sprint Retrospectiveinspect the way of working; plan improvements3 hours
    The three artifacts
    Each artifact comes with a commitment — the thing against which it is measured:
    

      

    • the Product Backlog is the ordered, changing list of what the product needs; its commitment is the Product Goal, the long-term objective of the product. Breaking items down and adding detail to them is called refinement; it is a continuous activity, not an event;
      • 

    • the Sprint Backlog contains the Sprint Goal, the items selected for the Sprint and the Developers' plan to deliver them; its commitment is the Sprint Goal;
      • 

    • the Increment is a usable step toward the Product Goal; each new Increment adds to all the previous ones and is verified with them, so that they work together; its commitment is the Definition of Done.
      • 

    

    One rule matters more than any other for a beginner: work counts only when it is Done.
    On the slide 18: Three artifacts, three commitments
    Three artifacts, three commitments
    • Product Backlog → commitment: Product Goal
    • Sprint Backlog → commitment: Sprint Goal
    • Increment → commitment: Definition of Done
    • Refinement: adding detail to backlog items — a continuous activity, not an event
    • Work counts only when it is Done
    Step 1Product BacklogProduct Goal
    Step 2Sprint BacklogSprint Goal
    Step 3IncrementDefinition of Done
    The Definition of Done
    

    Definition of Done — A formal description of the state the Increment must reach to meet the quality measures required for the product. The moment an item meets it, it becomes part of an Increment.
    

    

    The Guide is explicit about what happens otherwise: an item that does not meet the Definition of Done cannot be released, or even presented at the Sprint Review; it goes back to the Product Backlog. That is why the Definition of Done is a list of checks, written in advance and shared by the whole team — for example: reviewed by a teammate, unit tests written and passing, acceptance criteria met, merged into the main branch. “Almost done” does not exist in Scrum.
    

    Your team will write one. In Block 7, on November 3, your Definition of Done becomes the exit criteria of your test plan; in the December workshops, every Block is checked against it before you tag it.

    The Definition of Done

    • An item that fails it cannot be released, or even shown at the Sprint Review → back to the Product Backlog
    • Example: reviewed by a teammate · unit tests passing · acceptance criteria met · merged into main
    • “Almost done” does not exist
    • Block 7 (Nov 3): your Definition of Done becomes the exit criteria of the test plan

    The whole loop, and your course
    The figure shows the whole framework. Read it from the left: the Product Owner orders the Product Backlog; Sprint Planning selects items and writes the Sprint Goal; the Developers work through the Sprint, with one Daily Scrum each day; the Sprint Review inspects the Increment with the stakeholders; the Retrospective inspects the way of working; and the next Sprint starts at once.
    

    Your course already follows parts of this loop. Sprint 1 of your project runs from October 20 to November 8, and Sprint 2 from November 24 to December 20; in Scrum the next Sprint would start at once, but your course pauses between the two for the Mid-Term. The written stand-up that opens each December workshop — what is finished, what is in progress today, what blocks you — is a written form of the Daily Scrum. The exit ticket at the end of each class is a one-question retrospective.
    

    Now draw the loop yourselves.

    🏫Real-life example — QueueLess, Sprint 1: why only Done work counts
    Task. Team Falcon (fictional) runs the first two-week Sprint of QueueLess, the cafeteria pre-order app. The Product Owner has ordered four items; the Developers forecast 11 story points. The team follows the five events, and at the Sprint Review it checks every item against its Definition of Done.
    Relation to the lecture. It applies Lesson 2: the three accountabilities, the five events, the three artifacts with their commitments, and the rule that only Done work enters the Increment and counts in velocity.
    Sprint Planning writes the Sprint Goal — a student can order a sandwich and receive a pick-up number — and selects Q1 Browse today's menu (3 points), Q2 Pre-order a sandwich (5) and Q3 Get a pick-up number (3): 11 points, exactly the forecast. Q4 Staff see the queue (5) stays in the Product Backlog. On day 4, the Daily Scrum reveals an impediment — the test database is down — and the Scrum Master gets it restored the same day.
    

    On the last day, Q3 has one failing unit test. The team is tempted to present it as “90 % done”. The Definition of Done says no: Q3 returns to the top of the Product Backlog, the Increment contains Q1 and Q2, and the velocity is 8 points, not 11. At the Retrospective, the team decides to write each unit test before its code — Test-Driven Development, the next lesson.

    demo2_queueless_sprint.pyPython 3 · standard library only · fictional data
    Task. Move items from the Product Backlog to the Sprint Backlog until the forecast is reached, run ten Daily Scrums, inspect every item against the Definition of Done at the Sprint Review — sending back any item that fails a check — and compute the velocity from the Done items only.
    Relation to the lecture. Lesson 2: the events change the artifacts; the Definition of Done decides what enters the Increment; velocity counts only Done work.
    1"""CS 330 · Class 4 · Lesson 2 — demo2_queueless_sprint.py23Task: Team Falcon (fictional) runs Sprint 1 of QueueLess, the cafeteria4pre-order app. The program follows the five Scrum events in order: Sprint5Planning moves items from the Product Backlog to the Sprint Backlog until the6Developers' forecast is reached; the Daily Scrums run for ten working days; the7Sprint Review inspects every item against the Definition of Done — an item that8fails one check goes back to the Product Backlog; the Sprint Retrospective9measures the velocity and chooses one improvement for the next Sprint.1011Relation to the lecture: Lesson 2 names three accountabilities, five events and12three artifacts with their commitments. The program shows the artifacts change13during the events, and why only Done work counts in the Increment and in velocity.1415Fictional data only (Legal Notice, sections 6.7 and 18.2). Runs with any Python 3:16    python3 demo2_queueless_sprint.py17"""1819# The Product Backlog, already ordered by the Product Owner: each item is a tuple (identifier, title, story points).20product_backlog = [("Q1", "Browse today's menu", 3), ("Q2", "Pre-order a sandwich", 5), ("Q3", "Get a pick-up number", 3), ("Q4", "Staff see the queue", 5)]21# The Developers' forecast for this Sprint, in story points, agreed during Sprint Planning.22forecast = 1123# The Sprint Goal: one sentence, written at Sprint Planning, that says why this Sprint is worth doing.24sprint_goal = "a student can order a sandwich and receive a pick-up number"25# The Definition of Done: the four checks that every item must pass before it can be part of the Increment.26definition_of_done = ["peer review", "unit tests passing", "acceptance criteria met", "merged into main"]27# The result of each check for each selected item at the end of the Sprint (True = passed); item Q3 has one failing unit test.28check_results = {"Q1": [True, True, True, True], "Q2": [True, True, True, True], "Q3": [True, False, True, True]}29# Print the Sprint Goal first, because Sprint Planning starts with the question "why is this Sprint valuable?".30print(f"Sprint Planning: Sprint Goal = {sprint_goal}")31# The Sprint Backlog starts empty; Sprint Planning fills it.32sprint_backlog = []33# Keep a running total of the story points selected so far.34selected = 035# Walk through a copy of the Product Backlog from the top, because items will be removed from the original list inside the loop.36for item in list(product_backlog):37    # Stop as soon as the next item would take the total above the forecast.38    if selected + item[2] > forecast:39        # Leave the loop; the remaining items stay in the Product Backlog for a later Sprint.40        break41    # Remove the item from the Product Backlog.42    product_backlog.remove(item)43    # Add the same item to the Sprint Backlog.44    sprint_backlog.append(item)45    # Add its story points to the running total.46    selected += item[2]47    # Report the selection and the new total.48    print(f"Sprint Planning: {item[0]} {item[1]} ({item[2]} points) -> Sprint Backlog, total {selected}")49# Simulate the ten working days of a two-week Sprint; each day starts with a 15-minute Daily Scrum.50for day in range(1, 11):51    # On day 4 the Developers report an impediment at the Daily Scrum.52    if day == 4:53        # Print that Daily Scrum: the Scrum Master is accountable for causing the impediment to be removed.54        print(f"Daily Scrum day {day}: impediment - the test database is down; the Scrum Master gets it restored")55# After the loop, report how many Daily Scrums were held (the loop variable now holds the last day).56print(f"Daily Scrums held: {day}, 15 minutes each")57# The Increment starts empty; the Sprint Review decides what goes into it.58increment = []59# Inspect every Sprint Backlog item against the Definition of Done.60for item in sprint_backlog:61    # An item is Done only if every one of its checks passed.62    if all(check_results[item[0]]):63        # A Done item becomes part of the Increment.64        increment.append(item)65        # Report it.66        print(f"Sprint Review: {item[0]} meets the Definition of Done -> Increment")67    # At least one check failed.68    else:69        # Find the name of the first failed check, so that the report says exactly why the item is not Done.70        failed = definition_of_done[check_results[item[0]].index(False)]71        # An item that is not Done goes back to the top of the Product Backlog, where the Product Owner can reorder it.72        product_backlog.insert(0, item)73        # Report it.74        print(f"Sprint Review: {item[0]} is not Done (check failed: {failed}) -> back to the Product Backlog")75# Velocity counts only the story points of the items in the Increment, not of the items that were started.76velocity = sum(item[2] for item in increment)77# Sprint Retrospective: report the velocity against the forecast and record one improvement for the next Sprint.78print(f"Sprint Retrospective: velocity {velocity} of {forecast} forecast; improvement - write each unit test before its code")
    Execution steps — click one to go back to it
      Variables after this step
      Output
      Step-by-step explanation
      1. The first five lines create the data of the Sprint: the ordered Product Backlog (identifier, title, points), the forecast of 11 points, the Sprint Goal, the four checks of the Definition of Done, and the result of each check for each item.
      2. Sprint Planning starts by printing the Sprint Goal — the “why” comes first. Then sprint_backlog and the running total selected start at empty and zero.
      3. The selection loop walks through a copy of the Product Backlog. The copy matters: the loop removes items from the original list, and removing items from a list while looping over it skips elements. For each item the if asks whether adding its points would take the total above the forecast; Q1, Q2 and Q3 fit (3 + 5 + 3 = 11), Q4 would not, so break ends the selection.
      4. The Daily Scrum loop runs ten times, one working day each. Only day 4 prints something: the impediment and the Scrum Master's action. After the loop, one line confirms the ten Daily Scrums.
      5. The Sprint Review loop inspects the three selected items. all(...) is true only if every check passed: Q1 and Q2 join the Increment. For Q3, index(False) finds the first failed check — “unit tests passing” — and insert(0, item) puts Q3 back at the top of the Product Backlog.
      6. The velocity sums the points of the Increment only: 3 + 5 = 8. The forecast was 11; the 3 points of Q3 count zero because Q3 is not Done.
      7. The Retrospective line reports velocity against forecast and records one improvement. In the visualisation, watch the cards move between the three columns and the event strip advance from Planning to Retrospective.

      Q2.1
      Multiple-choice question
      Who is accountable for ordering the Product Backlog? (one right answer)
      • ✘ Wrong — No. The Scrum Master answers for the team's effectiveness and for Scrum itself, not for the order of the backlog.
      • ✔ Right — Yes. The Product Owner orders the Product Backlog to maximise the value of the product.
      • ✘ Wrong — No. The Developers plan the Sprint; the order of the Product Backlog is the Product Owner's decision.
      • ✘ Wrong — No. Stakeholders give feedback at the Review; the Product Owner decides the order.
      Hint: Which accountability is about maximising the value of the product?
      Q2.2
      Multiple-choice question
      For a one-month Sprint, what is the maximum timebox of the Sprint Retrospective? (one right answer)
      • ✘ Wrong — No. 15 minutes is the Daily Scrum.
      • ✔ Right — Yes. The 2020 Scrum Guide sets the Retrospective at a maximum of three hours for a one-month Sprint.
      • ✘ Wrong — No. Four hours is the maximum of the Sprint Review.
      • ✘ Wrong — No. Eight hours is the maximum of Sprint Planning.
      Hint: Recall the table of the five events: the Retrospective has neither the longest nor the shortest timebox.
      Q2.3
      Multiple-choice question
      In QueueLess Sprint 1, the third item, “Get a pick-up number”, has one failing unit test on the last day. What does Scrum say? (one right answer)
      • ✘ Wrong — No. An item that is not Done cannot even be presented at the Sprint Review.
      • ✔ Right — Yes. Not Done means back to the Product Backlog; its points do not count in the velocity.
      • ✘ Wrong — No. A Sprint has a fixed length; it is not extended to finish an item.
      • ✘ Wrong — No. Velocity counts only the points of Done items: 8, not 11.
      Hint: What is the rule for an item that does not meet the Definition of Done?
      Q2.4
      Multiple-choice question
      Which commitment belongs to the Sprint Backlog? (one right answer)
      • ✘ Wrong — No. The Product Goal is the commitment of the Product Backlog.
      • ✘ Wrong — No. The Definition of Done is the commitment of the Increment.
      • ✔ Right — Yes. The Sprint Backlog contains the Sprint Goal, the selected items and the plan.
      • ✘ Wrong — No. Velocity is a measure some teams use; it is not a commitment of any Scrum artifact.
      Hint: Each artifact has exactly one commitment.
      Q2.5
      Multiple-select question — choose every right answer
      Which statements about the Daily Scrum are true? (2 right answers)
      • ✔ Right — True: the same short timebox whatever the length of the Sprint.
      • ✔ Right — True: that is its purpose in the 2020 Guide.
      • ✘ Wrong — False: it is an event for the Developers to plan their next day, not a report.
      • ✘ Wrong — False: the Review inspects the outcome with the stakeholders at the end of the Sprint.
      • ✘ Wrong — False: it is held every working day, so that the plan is inspected and adapted daily.
      • ✘ Wrong — False: it is 15 minutes.
      Hint: Who is it for, how long is it, and what does it inspect?

      Which of these are events of the 2020 Scrum Guide? (3 right answers)

      • ✔ Right — Yes: inspect the outcome with the stakeholders.
      • ✔ Right — Yes: inspect the way of working.
      • ✘ Wrong — No: refinement is a continuous activity, not an event.
      • ✘ Wrong — No: the 2020 Guide has no such event.
      • ✘ Wrong — No: the Increment is an artifact.

      Part C
      Engineering practices, flow and planning
      0:26–0:48
      Goal of the lesson. Describe the values and the core practices of XP (Extreme Programming); explain the red–green–refactor cycle of TDD (Test-Driven Development); describe a Kanban board, a WIP (work in progress) limit and a pull system; use Little's Law to relate work in progress, throughput and cycle time.
      Extreme Programming
      

      Extreme Programming (XP) — An agile method created by Kent Beck in the late 1990s and described in his book Extreme Programming Explained (1999; second edition, with Cynthia Andres, 2004). It takes engineering practices that were already known to work and applies them all the time: if reviewing code is useful, review every line as it is written; if testing is useful, write the test before the code.
      

      

      The second edition names five values: communication, simplicity, feedback, courage and respect. Your textbook describes the XP (Extreme Programming) process as four framework activities: planning, in which the customer writes user stories and gives each one a value while the team estimates their cost; a simple design; coding in pairs, with the tests written first; and testing, with automated unit tests run on every change and acceptance tests written from the stories.
      On the slide 24: Extreme Programming: values and process
      Extreme Programming: values and process
      • Kent Beck, late 1990s; Extreme Programming Explained (1999; 2nd edition with Cynthia Andres, 2004)
      • Known good practices, applied all the time
      • Five values: communication · simplicity · feedback · courage · respect
      • Process: planning with user stories → simple design → coding in pairs, tests first → testing (unit + acceptance)
      Step 1Planninguser stories, value and cost
      Step 2Designkeep it simple
      Step 3Codingpairs, tests first
      Step 4Testingunit and acceptance tests
      Stories, small releases, pairs
      

      user story — A short description of a capability, written from the point of view of the person who wants it: As a ⟨kind of user⟩, I want ⟨a goal⟩, so that ⟨a benefit⟩.
      

      

      Ron Jeffries, one of the first XP (Extreme Programming) practitioners, described a story as three parts: the card that names it, the conversation that adds the detail, and the confirmation — the tests that decide whether it is done. The card is short on purpose; the details are agreed in the conversation and recorded in the tests.
      

      

      small release — Putting a working, tested version of the software in the users' hands frequently, so that their feedback arrives while it can still change the plan.
      

      pair programming — Two developers work at one computer: the driver writes the code; the navigator reviews each line as it is written and thinks about the next steps. They swap roles often.
      

      

      An experiment with university students by Laurie Williams and her colleagues, published in 2000, found that pairs produced code with fewer defects for somewhat more total effort than programmers working alone; later studies found the same two effects, with sizes that vary from study to study. In Lab 07, on November 3, you will implement your first stories in pairs and swap the keyboard every ten minutes.
      On the slide 25: XP (Extreme Programming) practices (1/2): stories, small releases, pairs
      XP (Extreme Programming) practices (1/2): stories, small releases, pairs
      • User story: As a ⟨user⟩, I want ⟨goal⟩, so that ⟨benefit⟩
      • Card · conversation · confirmation (Ron Jeffries)
      • Small release: working, tested software in users' hands often
      • Pair programming: driver writes, navigator reviews each line; swap often
      • Studies since about 2000: fewer defects, somewhat more total effort
      • Lab 07 (Nov 3): first stories in pairs, keyboard swapped every 10 minutes
      User storyAs a student, I want to send a study request, so that we can prepare the Mid-Term together.
      Small releasefeedback arrives while the plan can still change
      Pair programmingone keyboard, two people, roles swapped often
      Test first, refactor, integrate continuously
      

      Test-Driven Development (TDD) — A cycle repeated every few minutes: write one automated test for behaviour that does not exist yet and watch it fail (red); write the smallest code that makes it pass (green); then improve the structure of the code without changing its behaviour (refactor).
      

      refactoring — Changing the internal structure of code without changing what it does from the outside, so that it becomes easier to read and to change.
      

      

      The tests written in TDD (Test-Driven Development) are what make refactoring safe: if a change alters the behaviour, a test fails at once.
      

      

      continuous integration (CI) — A practice in which every developer merges small changes into the shared main branch at least once a day, and every merge starts an automated build and test run, so that integration problems are found within minutes, not weeks.
      

      

      These three practices depend on each other: tests make refactoring safe, refactoring keeps the design simple enough to test, and continuous integration runs every test on every change. In Lab 07 you will write one failing test first, then the code; on November 24 you will see a pipeline that runs your tests on every push.
      On the slide 26: XP (Extreme Programming) practices (2/2): test first, refactor, integrate
      XP (Extreme Programming) practices (2/2): test first, refactor, integrate
      • TDD (Test-Driven Development): red (a failing test) → green (smallest code that passes) → refactor (better structure, same behaviour)
      • Refactoring: change the internal structure, not the external behaviour
      • Continuous integration: merge small changes to main at least daily; every merge builds and tests
      • They depend on each other: tests make refactoring safe; integration runs all the tests

      Kanban
      Kanban comes from manufacturing — the Japanese word means a signal card, used in Toyota's production system — and was adapted to knowledge work, software included, by David J. Anderson in the 2000s. Two guides describe it today: The Kanban Guide↗scan, by John Coleman and Daniel Vacanti (May 2025 edition), and Kanban University's Official Guide to The Kanban Method↗scan. Both start from the same ideas.
      

      

      Kanban board — A board with one column per step of the workflow — for example Ready, Doing, Review, Done — on which each card is one work item, so that everyone can see where every item is.
      

      work-in-progress limit — The maximum number of work items allowed in a column, or per person, at the same time; it is usually called a WIP (work in progress) limit.
      

      pull system — A rule that a new item may start only when the step that will work on it has free capacity under its limit: the next step pulls work in; the previous step does not push it.
      

      

      Kanban has no Sprints and no prescribed roles. It changes the way of working one rule at a time: make the workflow visible, make the policies explicit (for example, when a card is allowed to move), limit the work in progress, and improve the flow with measurements.
      On the slide 27: Kanban: visualise the flow, limit the work in progress
      Kanban: visualise the flow, limit the work in progress
      • From Toyota's production system; adapted to software by David J. Anderson in the 2000s
      • Two current guides: The Kanban Guide (Coleman and Vacanti, May 2025) · Kanban University's Official Guide to The Kanban Method
      • Kanban board: one column per step, one card per item
      • WIP (work in progress) limit: maximum number of items in a column, or per person
      • Pull system: start an item only when there is room under the limit
      • No Sprints, no prescribed roles: improve one rule at a time

      Measuring the flow — Little's Law
      Kanban measures the flow with four numbers: the work in progress; the throughput; the cycle time; and the work item age — how long an unfinished item has already been in progress.
      

      

      throughput — The number of items finished per unit of time.
      

      cycle time — The time from the moment an item is started until the moment it is finished.
      

      

      Three of them are linked by Little's Law, a result of queueing theory proved by John Little in 1961 (Operations Research, 9(3)↗scan). For a stable system, over a long enough period:
      

      average work in progress = throughput × average cycle time.
      

      Solve it for the cycle time: average cycle time = average work in progress ÷ throughput. A team that finishes one card per day and keeps six cards open needs six days per card on average. The same team keeping only two cards open needs two days per card — and its throughput has not changed. That is what a WIP (work in progress) limit does, and the ClubLend demo measures it.
      On the slide 28: Measuring the flow: Little's Law
      Measuring the flow: Little's Law
      • Throughput: items finished per unit of time
      • Cycle time: time from the start of an item to its finish
      • Also tracked: work in progress, work item age
      • Little's Law (1961): average work in progress = throughput × average cycle time
      • 6 cards open, 1 finished per day → 6 days per card · 2 cards open → 2 days per card, same throughput
      average work in progress = throughput × average cycle time
      6 open ÷ 1 per day = 6 days · 2 open ÷ 1 per day = 2 days

      🏫Real-life example — ClubLend: the same six cards, with and without a limit
      Task. Team Owl (fictional) keeps the work of ClubLend on a Kanban board: catalogue search, borrow an item, return it, overdue reminder, waiting list and loan history — six cards in Ready, each one working day for the pair of Developers. The team compares two policies on the same six cards: start everything at once, or limit Doing to two cards.
      Relation to the lecture. It applies Lesson 3: the Kanban board, the WIP (work in progress) limit and the pull rule; it compares the two policies with the flow measures and Little's Law.
      With no limit, the pair starts all six cards on day 1 and spreads its effort over all of them: every card advances one sixth per day, all six finish together on day 6, and nothing reaches the club's members before then. With a limit of two cards in Doing, the pair works on two cards at a time: the first two are Done on day 2, the next two on day 4, the last two on day 6.
      

      The total time is the same — six days for six cards, a throughput of one card per day — but the average cycle time falls from 6 days to 2, and the members can try the first features on day 2 instead of day 6. Little's Law gives the same numbers: 1 card per day × 6 days = 6 cards in progress on average without a limit; 1 × 2 = 2 with it.

      🐍Demo program — ClubLend Kanban flow — no limit versus a limit of two
      demo3_clublend_kanban_flow.pyPython 3 · standard library only · fictional data
      Task. Simulate the same six cards day by day under two policies — no limit on Doing, then a limit of two cards — and print, for each policy, the board at the end of every day, the average cycle time, the throughput and the work in progress given by Little's Law.
      Relation to the lecture. Lesson 3: the pull rule and the WIP (work in progress) limit shorten the cycle time without lowering the throughput.
      1"""CS 330 · Class 4 · Lesson 3 — demo3_clublend_kanban_flow.py23Task: Team Owl (fictional) has six ClubLend cards in the Ready column of its4Kanban board (catalogue search, loan, return, reminder, and so on). A pair of5Developers can do six units of work per day, and every card needs six units.6The program runs the same six cards twice: once with no WIP (work in progress)7limit, so that every card is started on day 1, and once with a WIP (work in8progress) limit of 2 cards in Doing. For each9policy it prints the board day by day, then the cycle time, the throughput and10the average work in progress given by Little's Law.1112Relation to the lecture: Lesson 3 says that limiting work in progress shortens13cycle time without lowering throughput. The program measures exactly that, with14the pull rule of Kanban: a new card is started only when Doing is below its limit.1516Fictional data only (Legal Notice, sections 6.7 and 18.2). Runs with any Python 3:17    python3 demo3_clublend_kanban_flow.py18"""1920# Units of work that each card needs before it is Done (one unit is one sixth of the pair's working day).21WORK_PER_CARD = 622# Units of work the pair of Developers completes in one day; the units are shared equally among the cards in Doing.23CAPACITY_PER_DAY = 6242526# Define a function that simulates one policy; wip_limit is the WIP (work in progress) limit, the maximum number of cards in Doing, or None for no limit.27def simulate(wip_limit):28    # Text label of the policy, used at the start of every printed line.29    label = "no limit" if wip_limit is None else f"limit {wip_limit}"30    # The six cards waiting in the Ready column, highest priority first.31    ready = ["C1", "C2", "C3", "C4", "C5", "C6"]32    # Dictionary of the cards in Doing: card name -> units of work still to do.33    doing = {}34    # Dictionary: card name -> day on which the card was pulled into Doing.35    started = {}36    # Dictionary: card name -> day on which the card reached Done.37    finished = {}38    # Day counter; the simulation advances one working day at a time.39    day = 040    # Repeat while at least one card is still waiting or still in progress.41    while ready or doing:42        # Move to the next working day.43        day += 144        # Pull rule: start cards from Ready while Doing has room under the limit (with no limit, always).45        while ready and (wip_limit is None or len(doing) < wip_limit):46            # Take the highest-priority card from the top of Ready.47            card = ready.pop(0)48            # Put it in Doing with all of its work still to do.49            doing[card] = WORK_PER_CARD50            # Remember the day it was started, to compute its cycle time later.51            started[card] = day52        # Share the day's capacity equally among the cards in Doing (integer division: whole units only).53        share = CAPACITY_PER_DAY // len(doing)54        # Work on every card in Doing; iterate over a copy because finished cards are removed inside the loop.55        for card in list(doing):56            # Subtract today's share from the work still to do on this card.57            doing[card] -= share58            # A card with no work left is Done.59            if doing[card] <= 0:60                # Remove it from Doing.61                del doing[card]62                # Record the day it reached Done.63                finished[card] = day64        # Print the board at the end of the day: the cards in Doing and how many cards are Done.65        print(f"{label} | day {day}: Doing {sorted(doing)} | Done {len(finished)}")66    # Cycle time of each card: days from start to finish, both days included.67    cycle = {card: finished[card] - started[card] + 1 for card in finished}68    # Return the label, the cycle times, the finishing days and the total number of days.69    return label, cycle, finished, day707172# Run the two policies of the lecture, one after the other.73for limit in [None, 2]:74    # Simulate this policy and unpack the four results.75    label, cycle, finished, days = simulate(limit)76    # Average cycle time over the six cards, in days.77    avg_cycle = sum(cycle.values()) / len(cycle)78    # Throughput: cards finished per day over the whole run.79    throughput = len(cycle) / days80    # Little's Law: average work in progress = throughput x average cycle time.81    avg_wip = throughput * avg_cycle82    # The first day on which any card reached Done, i.e. the first moment users could get something.83    first_done = min(finished.values())84    # Print the summary of this policy.85    print(f"{label}: all done after {days} days | first card done on day {first_done} | average cycle time {avg_cycle:.1f} days | throughput {throughput:.1f} cards/day | Little's Law work in progress {avg_wip:.1f}")

        Step-by-step explanation
        1. Two constants fix the size of the problem: every card needs 6 units of work, and the pair completes 6 units per day. One card therefore needs one pair-day if the pair works on nothing else.
        2. The function simulate(wip_limit) runs one policy. It creates the Ready list, an empty Doing dictionary (card → units still to do), and two dictionaries that record the start day and the finish day of every card.
        3. The outer while loop advances one day at a time while any card is waiting or in progress. At the start of each day, the inner while is the pull rule: it moves cards from Ready to Doing while Doing is below the limit — with None, it moves all of them on day 1.
        4. The day's capacity is shared equally: 6 // len(doing) gives 1 unit per card when six cards are open, 3 units when two are open. The for loop subtracts the share from every open card and moves finished cards to Done, recording the finish day.
        5. After the loop, a dictionary comprehension computes each card's cycle time: finish day − start day + 1, because both days count.
        6. The main loop runs both policies and computes the average cycle time, the throughput (cards ÷ days) and Little's Law (throughput × average cycle time). Compare the two summary lines: same 6 days and same throughput, but cycle time 6.0 against 2.0, and the first card Done on day 6 against day 2.
        7. In the visualisation, the board shows the cards moving and their progress bars filling; the chart below adds one point per day. The rust line (no limit) stays at zero until day 6; the teal line (limit 2) rises every second day.

        Q3.1
        Multiple-choice question
        In TDD (Test-Driven Development), what does the developer write first? (one right answer)
        • ✘ Wrong — No. In TDD (Test-Driven Development) the code comes second, only to make a failing test pass.
        • ✔ Right — Yes. The failing test (red) defines the next small piece of behaviour.
        • ✘ Wrong — No. Documentation is not part of the red–green–refactor cycle.
        • ✘ Wrong — No. Refactoring is the third step, after the test passes.
        Hint: Red comes before green.
        Q3.2
        Multiple-choice question
        Two developers share one computer: one writes the code, the other reviews each line and thinks about the next steps. This practice is… (one right answer)
        • ✘ Wrong — No. Refactoring improves the structure of existing code; it does not describe two people at one computer.
        • ✔ Right — Yes. The driver writes, the navigator reviews and plans; they swap often.
        • ✘ Wrong — No. Continuous integration is about merging and testing every change automatically.
        • ✘ Wrong — No. Planning poker is an estimation technique (Lesson 4).
        Hint: Driver and navigator.
        Q3.3
        Multiple-choice question
        A team finishes 2 cards per day and keeps 8 cards in progress on average. By Little's Law, the average cycle time is… (one right answer)
        • ✘ Wrong — No. 16 is 8 × 2: the formula multiplies throughput by cycle time, not work in progress by throughput.
        • ✔ Right — Yes. 8 cards ÷ 2 cards per day = 4 days.
        • ✘ Wrong — No. 6 is 8 − 2; Little's Law divides.
        • ✘ Wrong — No. 0.25 is 2 ÷ 8, the division inverted.
        Hint: Cycle time = work in progress ÷ throughput.
        Q3.4
        Multiple-choice question
        In the ClubLend demo, what changed when Doing was limited to two cards? (one right answer)
        • ✘ Wrong — No. Both policies finish 6 cards in 6 days: 1 card per day.
        • ✔ Right — Yes. Same throughput, a third of the cycle time, and the first cards were Done on day 2 instead of day 6.
        • ✘ Wrong — No. Both policies need six days in total.
        • ✘ Wrong — No. The cycle time and the first delivery changed.
        Hint: Compare the two summary lines of the output.
        Q3.5
        Multiple-select question — choose every right answer
        Which statements about refactoring are true? (2 right answers)
        • ✔ Right — True: that is the definition.
        • ✔ Right — True: this is why TDD (Test-Driven Development) and refactoring go together.
        • ✘ Wrong — False: a new feature changes the behaviour; refactoring does not.
        • ✘ Wrong — False: in XP (Extreme Programming) it happens every few minutes, as the third step of the cycle.
        • ✘ Wrong — False: Kanban prescribes no engineering practice and forbids none.
        • ✘ Wrong — False: refactoring concerns code, not requirements.
        Hint: What changes, what must stay the same, and what makes it safe?
        Q3.6
        Multiple-select question — choose every right answer
        Which of these are practices of the Kanban method? (3 right answers)
        • ✔ Right — Yes: the board makes every item's step visible.
        • ✔ Right — Yes: WIP (work in progress) limits are the core of the method.
        • ✔ Right — Yes: written rules say when a card may move.
        • ✘ Wrong — No: Sprints belong to Scrum; Kanban is a continuous flow.
        • ✘ Wrong — No: Kanban prescribes no roles.
        • ✘ Wrong — No: Kanban does not require estimates; it measures the flow.
        Hint: Kanban has no Sprints and no prescribed roles.
        Goal of the lesson. Check a user story with INVEST (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable); write acceptance criteria in the Given/When/Then form; explain story points and planning poker; compute the number of Sprints from the velocity; read a burndown chart.
        Good user stories — INVEST (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable)
        A backlog is only as useful as its stories. In 2003 Bill Wake proposed six checks, remembered by the acronym INVEST (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable) (his original article↗scan):
        

          

        • Independent — the story can be built and delivered without waiting for another story;
          • 

        • Negotiable — it states a need, not a contract; the details are agreed in conversation;
          • 

        • Valuable — it delivers something that a user or a customer values;
          • 

        • Estimable — the team understands it well enough to estimate it;
          • 

        • Small — it fits comfortably inside one Sprint;
          • 

        • Testable — someone can write a test that decides whether it is done.
          • 

        

        Compare two stories for StudyBuddy. “The system shall have a database of study sessions.” has no user, no benefit, and no test a user could run: it is a task, not a story. “As a student, I want to send a study request to a classmate of the same course, so that we can prepare the Mid-Term together.” has a user, a goal, a benefit, and a test you can already imagine.
        On the slide 32: Good user stories: INVEST (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable)

        • Strong: “As a student, I want to send a study request to a classmate of the same course, so that we can prepare the Mid-Term together.”

        Acceptance criteria
        

        acceptance criteria — The conditions that a story must satisfy to be accepted, written before the work starts; they are the “confirmation” part of the story.
        

        

        A common format comes from BDD (Behaviour-Driven Development), introduced by Dan North in 2006:
        

          

        • Given a starting situation,
          • 

        • When the user performs an action,
          • 

        • Then the system produces an observable result.
          • 

        

        For the study request: given I am logged in and Ana is enrolled in CS 330, when I send Ana a study request for Thursday at 14:00, then Ana sees the request in her list, and I see its status as “pending”. A second criterion covers what must not happen: given Ana has blocked requests, when I send one, then the request is refused with a message.
        

        Each criterion becomes a test in Block 7. And in Lab 05 next week, every requirement you write will trace back to one of your stories.
        On the slide 33: Acceptance criteria: Given, When, Then
        Acceptance criteria: Given, When, Then
        • Acceptance criteria: conditions for accepting a story, written before the work
        • Format from BDD (Behaviour-Driven Development), introduced by Dan North in 2006: Given a situation · When an action · Then an observable result
        • Given I am logged in and Ana is in CS 330, when I send Ana a request for Thursday 14:00, then she sees it and I see “pending”
        • Given Ana blocks requests, when I send one, then it is refused with a message
        • Each criterion → a test in Block 7 · every requirement of Lab 05 traces back to a story
        GivenI am logged in and Ana is enrolled in CS 330
        WhenI send Ana a study request for Thursday at 14:00

        Story points and planning poker
        

        story point — A unit of relative size: it combines the effort, the complexity and the uncertainty of a story, compared with the team's other stories. It is not a number of hours.
        

        

        Teams that estimate in points rather than hours give two reasons: people tend to compare two tasks more reliably than they predict the duration of one, and the points stay valid when the team becomes faster.
        

        

        planning poker — An estimation technique: each member holds cards with the values 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20, 40 and 100, plus a “?”; the Product Owner reads a story; everyone picks a card in silence; all the cards are shown at the same time; the highest and the lowest estimators explain their reasons; the team votes again until the estimates converge.
        

        

        James Grenning set out the technique in 2002, and Mike Cohn made it widely known with his 2005 book Agile Estimating and Planning (Mountain Goat Software↗scan). The gaps between the card values grow because the uncertainty of an estimate grows with its size: nobody can tell a story of 21 points from one of 22, so the deck does not offer that choice. Showing the cards together prevents the first opinion from influencing the others, and the discussion between the highest and the lowest estimate is where hidden work is found.
        On the slide 34: Story points and planning poker
        Story points and planning poker
        • Story point: relative size = effort + complexity + uncertainty, compared with the team's other stories — not hours
        • People tend to compare two tasks more reliably than they predict one duration
        • Planning poker: cards 0 · 1 · 2 · 3 · 5 · 8 · 13 · 20 · 40 · 100 · ?
        • Choose in silence → reveal together → highest and lowest explain → vote again
        • James Grenning (2002); Mike Cohn, Agile Estimating and Planning (2005)
        1235813?
        Velocity — Numbers corner
        

        velocity — The number of story points of the items that met the Definition of Done in one Sprint. Items that were started but are not Done count zero.
        

        

        Velocity is measured, not promised. After two or three Sprints, the team uses its average velocity to forecast:
        

        sprints needed = ⌈ remaining story points ÷ velocity ⌉
        

        The brackets mean “rounded up”: a partial Sprint still costs a whole Sprint. Example: 45 points remain and the velocity is 15 points per Sprint; 45 ÷ 15 = 3 Sprints. Second example: 18 ready points at 8 points per Sprint gives 2.25, rounded up to 3 Sprints.
        

        Two warnings. Velocity belongs to one team: points are relative to that team's own stories, so comparing the velocities of two teams compares two different units. And velocity is a planning tool, not a performance target: a team rewarded for a high velocity soon inflates its estimates, and the forecast stops meaning anything.
        On the slide 35: Velocity — Numbers corner
        Velocity — Numbers corner
        • Velocity: story points of the items that met the Definition of Done in one Sprint
        • Measured, not promised: items started but not Done count zero
        • Sprints needed = ⌈ remaining points ÷ velocity ⌉ (round up)
        • 45 points ÷ 15 per Sprint = 3 Sprints · 18 ÷ 8 = 2.25 → 3 Sprints
        • Velocity belongs to one team: do not compare teams
        • A planning tool, not a target: a rewarded velocity inflates estimates
        Sprints needed = ⌈ remaining story points ÷ velocity ⌉
        45 ÷ 15 = 3 Sprints · 18 ÷ 8 = 2.25 → 3 Sprints
        Reading a burndown chart
        

        burndown chart — A chart of the work remaining in a Sprint, in story points, against the days of the Sprint, with an ideal straight line from the committed points on day 0 to zero on the last day.
        

        

        Two rules are enough to read it. A point above the ideal line means the team is behind; a point below means it is ahead. And because a story counts only when it is Done, the actual line falls in steps, not smoothly. In StudyBuddy's Sprint 1 the line stays at 8 points for two days, falls to 5 when the 3-point story is Done on day 3, stays flat until day 8, and reaches zero on day 9. A long flat stretch is a signal to look for a blocked or an oversized story — at the Daily Scrum, not at the end of the Sprint.
        

        Some teams prefer a burnup chart, which shows the work completed rising toward the total; it makes a change of scope visible, because the total line moves.
        On the slide 36: Reading a burndown chart
        Reading a burndown chart
        • Burndown chart: points remaining against the days of the Sprint, with an ideal straight line
        • Above the ideal line = behind · below = ahead
        • The actual line falls in steps: a story counts only when Done
        • A long flat stretch: look for a blocked or an oversized story — at the Daily Scrum
        • Burnup chart: work completed rising toward the total; shows changes of scope

        Task. Team Lynx (fictional) prepares Sprint 1 of StudyBuddy. After a round of planning poker it has eight stories. The team checks them against INVEST (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable), forecasts the number of Sprints with an assumed velocity, follows the burndown of Sprint 1, measures its real velocity and forecasts again.
        Relation to the lecture. It applies Lesson 4 — INVEST (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable) stories, acceptance criteria, story points, velocity, burndown — and the Numbers corner.
        Three of the eight stories are sent back. Rate a finished session has no acceptance criteria, so it is not testable. Manage everything about my profile received 13 points, more than the 8 points Team Lynx accepts for one story in a two-week Sprint: it bundles several features and must be split. Weekly summary e-mail has no estimate, because the team disagreed on what the summary contains — a sign that the conversation has not happened yet. A program can check only three letters of INVEST (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable) — Estimable, Small, Testable; whether a story is independent, negotiable and valuable needs people.
        

        Five stories are ready, worth 18 points. With an assumed velocity of 8 points per two-week Sprint, the forecast is ⌈18 ÷ 8⌉ = 3 Sprints. Sprint 1 commits the first two stories, 3 + 5 = 8 points. The burndown stays at 8 for two days, drops to 5 on day 3, stays flat while the 5-point story is in progress, and reaches 0 on day 9. Measured velocity: 8. With 10 points left, the new forecast is ⌈10 ÷ 8⌉ = 2 more Sprints.

Runs with any Python 3:16    python3 demo4_studybuddy_velocity_burndown.py17"""1819# Import ceil from the standard math module: a partial Sprint still needs a whole Sprint.20from math import ceil2122# The backlog after planning poker; each story is (title, story points or None if not estimated, has acceptance criteria).23stories = [24    # Story 1: estimated at 3 points, with acceptance criteria.25    ("Search study partners by course", 3, True),26    # Story 2: estimated at 5 points, with acceptance criteria.27    ("Send a study request", 5, True),28    # Story 3: estimated at 3 points, with acceptance criteria.29    ("Confirm or decline a request", 3, True),30    # Story 4: estimated at 5 points, with acceptance criteria.31    ("Book a study-room slot", 5, True),32    # Story 5: estimated at 2 points, with acceptance criteria.33    ("Cancel a session", 2, True),34    # Story 6: estimated at 3 points but nobody wrote its acceptance criteria yet.35    ("Rate a finished session", 3, False),36    # Story 7: 13 points, far too big for one Sprint; it bundles several features.37    ("Manage everything about my profile", 13, True),38    # Story 8: the team could not agree on an estimate, so it has no points.39    ("Weekly summary e-mail", None, True),40# Close the list of stories.41]42# Largest estimate accepted for one story; anything bigger must be split (the S, Small, of INVEST: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable).43MAX_POINTS = 844# The ready stories will be collected in this list.45ready = []46# Check every story against the three letters a program can test.47for title, points, has_criteria in stories:48    # E, Estimable: the team agreed on an estimate.49    if points is None:50        # Not estimable: report it and send it back to the team for a conversation.51        print(f"Story check: '{title}' fails E (Estimable) - discuss it, then estimate it again")52    # S, Small: the story fits comfortably in one Sprint.53    elif points > MAX_POINTS:54        # Too big: report it and ask for a split.55        print(f"Story check: '{title}' fails S (Small) - {points} points, split it into smaller stories")56    # T, Testable: acceptance criteria exist, so a test can decide when the story is done.57    elif not has_criteria:58        # Not testable: report it and ask for Given/When/Then criteria.59        print(f"Story check: '{title}' fails T (Testable) - write its Given/When/Then criteria")60    # The story passed E, S and T (Estimable, Small, Testable); I, N and V (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable) still need people to judge them.61    else:62        # Keep it as a ready story.63        ready.append((title, points))64# Total story points of the ready stories.65ready_points = sum(points for title, points in ready)66# Report how many stories are ready and their total.67print(f"Ready: {len(ready)} stories, {ready_points} points (Independent, Negotiable and Valuable still need a human check)")68# Velocity assumed before any Sprint has been measured, in points per two-week Sprint.69assumed_velocity = 870# Forecast: number of Sprints needed for the ready points, rounded up.71print(f"Forecast: {ready_points} points / {assumed_velocity} points per Sprint = {ceil(ready_points / assumed_velocity)} Sprints")72# Sprint 1 commitment: the first two ready stories (3 + 5 points).73committed = ready[0][1] + ready[1][1]74# Points still to do at the end of each of the ten working days of Sprint 1 (a story burns down only when it is Done).75remaining = [8, 8, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 0, 0]76# Follow the burndown day by day.77for day in range(1, 11):78    # Ideal remaining work, in tenths of a point, so that the comparison uses whole numbers: committed x (10 - day) / 10.79    ideal_tenths = committed * (10 - day)80    # Actual remaining work, also in tenths of a point.81    actual_tenths = remaining[day - 1] * 1082    # Above the ideal line means behind schedule, below means ahead, on the line means on track.83    status = "behind" if actual_tenths > ideal_tenths else ("ahead" if actual_tenths < ideal_tenths else "on track")84    # Print one point of the burndown chart.85    print(f"Burndown day {day:>2}: ideal {ideal_tenths / 10:.1f} | actual {remaining[day - 1]} | {status}")86# Measured velocity: the points that met the Definition of Done in Sprint 1.87velocity = committed - remaining[-1]88# Points left in the ready stories after Sprint 1.89left = ready_points - velocity90# New forecast with the measured velocity instead of the assumed one.91print(f"Measured velocity {velocity}; {left} points left -> {ceil(left / velocity)} more Sprints")
