          Variables after this step
          Output
          Step-by-step explanation
          1. The program imports ceil, because a partial Sprint costs a whole Sprint. The list stories holds eight tuples: title, points (or None when the team could not agree), and whether acceptance criteria exist.
          2. The for loop unpacks each tuple into three names and tests three letters in order: E (no estimate), S (more than 8 points), T (no criteria). The first failed test prints a message and moves to the next story; a story that passes all three is appended to ready.
          3. Watch the left panel of the visualisation: each story gets three badges, E, S and T. Three stories fail, one letter each; five pass. The remark printed after the loop is part of the lesson: independence, negotiability and value need human judgement.
          4. ready_points sums the points of the ready stories: 3 + 5 + 3 + 5 + 2 = 18. The forecast divides by the assumed velocity of 8 and rounds up: ⌈2.25⌉ = 3 Sprints.
          5. Sprint 1 commits the first two ready stories: 8 points. remaining lists the points left at the end of each of the ten days; a story lowers it only on the day it is Done, so the list has steps.
          6. The burndown loop computes the ideal value for each day in tenths of a point — 8 × (10 − day) — so that the comparison with the actual value uses whole numbers and never suffers from rounding. Above the ideal line is “behind”, below is “ahead”.
          7. The last three lines measure the velocity (8 − 0 = 8), the points left (18 − 8 = 10) and the new forecast (⌈10 ÷ 8⌉ = 2 more Sprints). In the chart, the red dots of the flat stretch show where a Daily Scrum should ask what blocks the 5-point story.

          Q4.1
          Multiple-choice question
          45 story points remain and the team's velocity is 15 points per Sprint. How many Sprints are needed? (one right answer)
          • ✘ Wrong — No. 2 Sprints of 15 points cover 30, not 45.
          • ✔ Right — Yes. 45 ÷ 15 = 3 exactly; no rounding is needed.
          • ✘ Wrong — No. 4 would be right only if a partial Sprint remained, for example with 46 points.
          • ✘ Wrong — No. 45 is the number of points, not of Sprints.
          Hint: Divide, then round up if needed.
          Q4.2
          Multiple-choice question
          In the StudyBuddy demo, which INVEST (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable) letter does “Manage everything about my profile” (13 points) fail? (one right answer)
          • ✘ Wrong — No. The story has an estimate, 13 points, so the team could size it.
          • ✔ Right — Yes. 13 points is more than Team Lynx's limit of 8 points per story: the story must be split.
          • ✘ Wrong — No. The story has acceptance criteria, so a test can decide when it is done.
          • ✘ Wrong — No. The story may well be valuable; its problem is its size, and a program cannot judge value.
          Hint: Look at the story's number of points and at Team Lynx's rule for one story.
          Q4.3
          Multiple-choice question
          Day 6 of a ten-day Sprint with 8 committed points: the burndown shows 5 points remaining, and the ideal line is at 3.2. The team is… (one right answer)
          • ✘ Wrong — No. Ahead would mean fewer points remaining than the ideal line, below 3.2.
          • ✔ Right — Yes. 5 is above 3.2: more work remains than the ideal line allows on day 6.
          • ✘ Wrong — No. On track would mean exactly 3.2 points remaining.
          • ✘ Wrong — No. 5 points still remain.
          Hint: Is the actual point above or below the ideal line?
          Q4.4
          Multiple-choice question
          Why do planning-poker players show their cards at the same time? (one right answer)
          • ✘ Wrong — No. Showing cards together does not save time; the discussion that follows takes longer.
          • ✔ Right — Yes. Simultaneous reveal keeps the estimates independent until the discussion starts.
          • ✘ Wrong — No. The Scrum Guide does not prescribe any estimation technique.
          • ✘ Wrong — No. The team converges on an estimate through discussion; nobody picks the highest.
          Hint: What would happen if the most senior person spoke first?
          Q4.5
          Multiple-select question — choose every right answer
          Which statements about velocity are true? (2 right answers)
          • ✔ Right — True: started items count zero.
          • ✔ Right — True: Sprints needed = ⌈remaining points ÷ velocity⌉.
          • ✘ Wrong — False: points are relative to each team's own stories.
          • ✘ Wrong — False: a target velocity leads to inflated estimates.
          • ✘ Wrong — False: QueueLess forecast 11 and measured 8.
          • ✘ Wrong — False: it is measured in story points.
          Hint: What does it count, and what is it for?
          Q4.6
          Multiple-select question — choose every right answer
          Which are well-formed acceptance criteria for the story “send a study request”? (3 right answers)
          • ✔ Right — Correct: situation, action, observable result.
          • ✔ Right — Correct: it covers what must not happen.
          • ✔ Right — Correct: it covers a duplicate request, with a situation, an action and an observable result.
          • ✘ Wrong — Wrong: no situation, no action, nothing a test can check.
          • ✘ Wrong — Wrong: a design decision, not a condition of acceptance.
          • ✘ Wrong — Wrong: a priority, not an acceptance criterion.
          Hint: Each must describe a situation, an action and an observable result that a test can check.

          Part D
          Process improvement and the LO1 (Learning Outcome 1) debate
          0:48–1:00
          Goal of the lesson. Define software process improvement; describe the improvement cycle (assess, plan, improve, measure) and the IDEAL (Initiating, Diagnosing, Establishing, Acting, Learning) model; name and describe the CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) maturity levels; place ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission / Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers standard 12207) and the ISO/IEC 33000 (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission standards series 33000) family; argue for and against process improvement.
          What process improvement is, and where it comes from
          

          software process improvement (SPI) — A systematic effort to assess how an organisation develops software, find the weaknesses of that process, change it, and measure whether the change helped.
          

          

          Why would an organisation spend money on this? Because its process largely determines how predictable its schedules are and how many defects reach its users. An organisation that cannot describe how it works cannot repeat its successes or explain its failures. Clients know it: large public and private buyers of software often ask their suppliers for evidence of a mature process before they sign a contract.
          

          The field grew out of that kind of request. In 1984 the United States Department of Defense created the SEI (Software Engineering Institute), a research centre for software engineering. In 1986, at the request of the United States Air Force, which wanted a way to evaluate the software contractors it hired, Watts Humphrey began to write down a process maturity framework. It led to the SW-CMM (Capability Maturity Model for Software) in 1991, and to CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) from 2000. Since 2016 the model belongs to ISACA (the professional association formerly named Information Systems Audit and Control Association), through the CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) Institute↗scan; the current version is CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) V3.0 (version 3.0), released in 2023.
          On the slide 40: Software process improvement: what and why

          The improvement cycle
          Most improvement methods repeat the same cycle under different names: assess → plan → improve → measure, and then assess again.
          

            

          • Assess — compare the current practices with a model or a standard; the difference is the gap.
            • 

          • Plan — choose a few changes that close the most important part of the gap, each with an owner and a date.
            • 

          • Improve — introduce the changes, train the people, and use the changes on real work.
            • 

          • Measure — collect evidence that the change helped: fewer defects found late, a more accurate forecast, a shorter cycle time.
            • 

          

          The SEI (Software Engineering Institute) named its version IDEAL (Initiating, Diagnosing, Establishing, Acting, Learning) (McFeeley, 1996↗scan), after the first letters of its five phases. Initiating sets up the programme: a sponsor, goals, and the people who will run it. Diagnosing assesses the current process against a model and lists the gaps. Establishing chooses the priorities and writes the improvement plan. Acting pilots the changes, refines them and rolls them out. Learning measures the results and feeds the lessons into the next cycle; in the original 1996 handbook this fifth phase was called Leveraging. Your textbook lists the same steps as assessment and gap analysis, education and training, selection and justification, installation and migration, and evaluation, with risk management throughout. An older form of the same idea is the PDCA (Plan, Do, Check, Act) cycle of quality management. And you met the smallest form today: the Sprint Retrospective is one improvement cycle, run by one team, every Sprint.
          On the slide 41: The improvement cycle
          The improvement cycle
          • Assess — compare the practices with a model; the difference is the gap
          • Plan — a few changes for the most important part of the gap, with owners and dates
          • Improve — introduce the changes, train, use them on real work
          • Measure — evidence that the change helped
          • The SEI (Software Engineering Institute) model of 1996: IDEAL (Initiating, Diagnosing, Establishing, Acting, Learning)
          • The smallest improvement cycle: the Sprint Retrospective
          Assess→Plan→Improve→Measure↻ repeat
          The CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) maturity levels
          A maturity model describes the stages an organisation's process goes through, each stage defined by a set of practices. The official page of the CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) Institute↗scan lists six maturity levels, from 0 to 5; the table gives each one in a line.
          

          Two remarks. First, a maturity level describes the organisation's process, not the quality of one product: an organisation at level 3 can still deliver a poor product. Second, CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) also defines capability levels, from 0 to 3, for a single practice area — for example, how well an organisation performs configuration management — while the maturity levels, from 0 to 5, describe the organisation as a whole. An organisation obtains a level through an appraisal, led by an appraiser certified by the CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) Institute.
          On the slide 42: CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) maturity levels
          CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) maturity levels
          LevelNameWhat characterises it
          0Incompletework is improvised; it may or may not be finished
          1Initialwork gets done, but reactively; often late and over budget
          2Managedprojects are planned, performed, measured and controlled
          3Definedstandard processes for the organisation, tailored by each project
          4Quantitatively Managednumeric goals for quality and performance, managed with data
          5Optimizingcontinuous improvement based on data; quick adaptation
          The international standards: 12207 and the 33000 family
          One international standard and one family of standards cover the same ground as CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration).
          

          ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission / Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers standard 12207) — Systems and software engineering — Software life cycle processes — is the catalogue of the processes a software life cycle can contain, from acquisition and supply, through planning, requirements, design, implementation and verification, to operation, maintenance and retirement, each with its purpose and its expected outcomes. It says what each process must achieve, not how a team must work. Its second edition↗scan was published in April 2026 and replaced the 2017 edition↗scan. Last week's IEEE Std 1074 (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers Standard 1074) served a related purpose: assembling the life cycle of one project.
          

          The ISO/IEC 33000 (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission standards series 33000) family says how to assess a process. ISO/IEC 33001 (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission standard 33001) (2015↗scan) defines the concepts, and ISO/IEC 33020 (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission standard 33020) (2019↗scan) defines the scale of process capability levels: 0 incomplete, 1 performed, 2 managed, 3 established, 4 predictable, 5 innovating. The family replaced ISO/IEC 15504 (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission standard 15504), better known as SPICE (Software Process Improvement and Capability dEtermination).
          

          Side by side: 12207 lists the processes; the 33000 family measures how capable each process is; CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) groups practices into maturity levels for a whole organisation.

          The LO1 (Learning Outcome 1) debate — is it worth it?
          Here is the debate you will hold, with arguments, in the Final.
          

          For: a defined and measured process makes schedules and quality more predictable; it lets an organisation repeat what works and stop repeating what fails; new people learn the process from its description; clients can compare suppliers; and measurements show whether a change helped instead of leaving it to opinion.
          

          Against: assessments and appraisals cost time and money; a process can be written for the appraisal rather than used for the work; heavy documentation slows a small team and can contradict the agile values; and a maturity level says nothing direct about the quality of one particular product.
          

          A common position today combines the two: agile teams can adopt CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) practices without writing documents for their own sake. A Definition of Done is a quality-assurance practice; a burndown chart supports monitoring and control; one Git tag per Block is a simple form of configuration management. For a four-person team, running the improvement cycle matters more than a level; for a company that builds software for a government, the level may decide the contract. Keep that question for the Studio: is a maturity level worth it for your team — and what would you measure?

          🏫Real-life example — HabitHub: two improvement cycles to a level-2-style checklist
          Task. Team Wren (fictional) builds HabitHub: track daily habits and streaks, with a weekly report. The team answers, honestly, a six-practice checklist inspired by the practice areas that CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) expects at maturity level 2, then runs the improvement cycle — assess, plan, improve, measure — adopting at most two new practices per cycle.
          Relation to the lecture. It applies Lesson 5 — the improvement cycle and the maturity levels — at the scale of a four-person team, using practices the team will meet in Lab 05, Block 7 and the December workshops.
          The first assessment finds two practices in place: the team plans its work (project planning) and tags every Block (configuration management). Four are missing: requirements management, monitoring and control, quality assurance and measurement. The team can absorb two new practices per cycle without slowing its product work, so cycle 1 adopts Given/When/Then criteria for every story and a Kanban board updated at every stand-up; the measurement shows 4 of 6. Cycle 2 adopts a review of every file by a teammate before it is tagged, and the recording of velocity and test coverage every Sprint: 6 of 6.
          

          The checklist is a classroom simplification. A real CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) appraisal is led by a certified appraiser, examines many more practices, and asks for evidence that they are used — not for six yes-or-no answers. The cycle, however, is the real one.

          Task. Read Team Wren's six checklist answers, then repeat the improvement cycle until every practice is in place: assess the gap, plan at most two actions, adopt them, and measure how many practices are in place.
          Relation to the lecture. Lesson 5: the improvement cycle and the CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) maturity levels, at the scale of one student team.
          1"""CS 330 · Class 4 · Lesson 5 — demo5_habithub_spi_cycle.py23Task: Team Wren (fictional) builds HabitHub. It answers, honestly, a six-item4checklist inspired by the practice areas that CMMI (Capability Maturity Model5Integration) expects at maturity level 2, Managed. Then it runs the software6process improvement cycle — assess, plan, improve, measure — adopting at most7two new practices per cycle, until every practice of the checklist is in place.89Relation to the lecture: Lesson 5 — what software process improvement is, the10improvement cycle, and the CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration)11maturity levels. The checklist is a classroom12simplification: a real CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) appraisal is led by a certified appraiser and13examines far more evidence than six yes/no answers.1415Fictional data only (Legal Notice, sections 6.7 and 18.2). Runs with any Python 3:16    python3 demo5_habithub_spi_cycle.py17"""1819# The six practices of the classroom checklist, in a fixed order so that every report lists them the same way.20practices = ["requirements management", "project planning", "monitoring and control", "configuration management", "quality assurance", "measurement"]21# Team Wren's honest answers today: True means the practice is already part of how the team works.22in_place = {"requirements management": False, "project planning": True, "monitoring and control": False, "configuration management": True, "quality assurance": False, "measurement": False}23# One small, concrete improvement action for each practice; the plan step chooses among them.24actions = {25    # Requirements management: every story gets testable acceptance criteria (this becomes Lab 05 work).26    "requirements management": "write Given/When/Then criteria for every story",27    # Project planning: estimate and plan each Sprint.28    "project planning": "plan each Sprint with story points",29    # Monitoring and control: compare progress with the plan at every stand-up.30    "monitoring and control": "update the Kanban board at every stand-up",31    # Configuration management: identify every delivered version.32    "configuration management": "one Git tag per Block",33    # Quality assurance: a second person checks every work product.34    "quality assurance": "a teammate reviews every file before it is tagged",35    # Measurement: record numbers that show whether the process improves.36    "measurement": "record velocity and test coverage every Sprint",37# Close the dictionary of actions.38}39# The team can absorb at most two new practices per improvement cycle without slowing down its product work.40MAX_NEW_PER_CYCLE = 241# Number of practices on the checklist.42total = len(practices)43# Cycle counter.44cycle = 045# Repeat the improvement cycle while at least one practice is missing.46while not all(in_place.values()):47    # Start a new cycle.48    cycle += 149    # ASSESS: the gap is the list of practices that are not yet in place, in checklist order.50    gap = [name for name in practices if not in_place[name]]51    # Report the assessment: how many practices are in place and which ones are missing.52    print(f"Cycle {cycle} - assess: {total - len(gap)} of {total} in place; gap = {', '.join(gap)}")53    # PLAN: choose the first practices of the gap, at most two.54    plan = gap[:MAX_NEW_PER_CYCLE]55    # Report the plan as the concrete actions the team will take.56    print(f"Cycle {cycle} - plan: {'; '.join(actions[name] for name in plan)}")57    # IMPROVE: adopt each planned practice (in real life this takes the weeks between two assessments).58    for name in plan:59        # Mark the practice as in place.60        in_place[name] = True61    # MEASURE: count the practices in place after the improvement.62    count = sum(in_place.values())63    # Report the measurement, also as a percentage of the checklist rounded to the nearest whole number.64    print(f"Cycle {cycle} - measure: {count} of {total} in place ({round(count * 100 / total)}%)")65# Report the outcome: with every practice in place, this checklist's condition for level 2 is met.66print(f"After {cycle} cycles every practice of the checklist is in place: the checklist's condition for CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) maturity level 2, Managed, is met")
          Execution steps — click one to go back to it
            Variables after this step
            Output
            Step-by-step explanation
            1. The list practices fixes the order of the six checklist items; the dictionary in_place holds the team's honest answers; actions gives one small, concrete improvement for each practice.
            2. MAX_NEW_PER_CYCLE = 2 is a design decision of the team: more than two changes at once would slow the product work and make it harder to tell which change helped.
            3. The while not all(in_place.values()) loop is the cycle: it runs as long as at least one practice is missing. all() returns True only when every value is True.
            4. Assess: a list comprehension collects the practices that are not in place — the gap. Plan: the slice gap[:2] takes the first two. The printed plan is a list of actions, not of practice names, because an improvement is something people do.
            5. Improve: the inner for sets the planned practices to True. In a real team this step takes weeks; in the program it is one assignment.
            6. Measure: sum(in_place.values()) counts the True values, because Python treats True as 1. The percentage is rounded to the nearest whole number: 4 of 6 is 67 %.
            7. The loop runs twice: 2 → 4 → 6 practices. In the visualisation, follow the cycle wheel through its four phases, the tiles turning green, and the team marker climbing from level 1 to level 2 of the staircase when the checklist is complete.
            Run it on your own computer too: python3 demo5_habithub_spi_cycle.py (Legal Notice, section 10: run code only on equipment you own or are allowed to use).

            ✎Formative quiz — 4 multiple-choice and 2 multiple-select questions
            ⚑ This quiz is FORMATIVE, not summative: it is here to help you learn, nothing is recorded or sent anywhere, and it does NOT count towards your final grade. The graded assessments of CS 330 are the project Blocks with engagement (30 %), the Mid-Term (30 %, Tuesday, November 17) and the Final (40 %, Tuesday, January 19).
            Q5.1
            Multiple-choice question
            At which CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) maturity level are projects planned, performed, measured and controlled, while the processes are not yet standard across the organisation? (one right answer)
            • ✘ Wrong — No. At level 1 work gets done, but reactively, without planning and control.
            • ✔ Right — Yes. Level 2 manages each project; level 3 makes the processes standard for the organisation.
            • ✘ Wrong — No. Level 3 is precisely the level of organisation-wide standard processes.
            • ✘ Wrong — No. Level 5 improves continuously on top of quantitative management.
            Hint: Projects are managed one by one before the organisation defines one standard process.
            Q5.2
            Multiple-choice question
            Which standard is the catalogue of software life-cycle processes whose current edition was published in 2026? (one right answer)
            • ✘ Wrong — No. ISO/IEC 33020 (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission standard 33020) defines the capability levels used to assess processes.
            • ✔ Right — Yes. Its second edition, published in April 2026, replaced the 2017 edition.
            • ✘ Wrong — No. The Scrum Guide defines one framework; it is not an international standard.
            • ✘ Wrong — No. ISO/IEC 15504 (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission standard 15504), or SPICE (Software Process Improvement and Capability dEtermination), was replaced by the ISO/IEC 33000 (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission standards series 33000) family.
            Hint: One standard lists the processes; another measures their capability.
            Q5.3
            Multiple-choice question
            In the HabitHub demo, how many improvement cycles did Team Wren need, adopting at most two practices per cycle? (one right answer)
            • ✘ Wrong — No. Four practices were missing, and one cycle adopts at most two.
            • ✔ Right — Yes. Four missing practices, two per cycle: 2 → 4 → 6.
            • ✘ Wrong — No. The third assessment is never needed: after cycle 2 all six are in place.
            • ✘ Wrong — No. That would be one practice per cycle.
            Hint: How many practices were missing at the first assessment?
            Q5.4
            Multiple-choice question
            What does a CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) maturity level describe? (one right answer)
            • ✘ Wrong — No. A maturity level is about the process, not a guarantee for a product.
            • ✔ Right — Yes. It describes the organisation's way of working as a whole.
            • ✘ Wrong — No. CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) rates organisations, not individuals.
            • ✘ Wrong — No. Size is measured with metrics such as lines of code or function points.
            Hint: An organisation at level 3 can still deliver a poor product.
            Q5.5
            Multiple-select question — choose every right answer
            Which pairs correctly match a phase of the SEI (Software Engineering Institute)'s IDEAL (Initiating, Diagnosing, Establishing, Acting, Learning) model with a step of the generic improvement cycle — assess, plan, improve, measure? (2 right answers)
            • ✔ Right — Yes: Diagnosing compares the current process with a model and lists the gaps.
            • ✔ Right — Yes: Establishing chooses the priorities and writes the improvement plan.
            • ✘ Wrong — No: Initiating starts the programme — sponsorship, goals and the people who will run it.
            • ✘ Wrong — No: Acting pilots and rolls out the changes; it is the improve step.
            • ✘ Wrong — No: Learning measures the results and feeds the next cycle; it is the measure step.
            • ✘ Wrong — No: Leveraging is the 1996 name of the fifth phase, today Learning; it corresponds to measure, not improve.
            Hint: Follow the order of the phases: after the start-up phase, the first real step looks at the current process; the next one decides what to change.
            Q5.6
            Multiple-select question — choose every right answer
            Which arguments support process improvement in the LO1 (Learning Outcome 1) debate? (3 right answers)
            • ✔ Right — For: a defined, measured process can be repeated.
            • ✔ Right — For: evidence replaces opinion.
            • ✔ Right — For: a public scale gives buyers a common reference.
            • ✘ Wrong — No: a level describes the process, not one product.
            • ✘ Wrong — No: that is a criticism — a process that is written down but not used.
            • ✘ Wrong — No: appraisals cost time and money; that is an argument against.
            Hint: Three are benefits; three are either criticisms or false claims.

            Active break · Zen-break, then flash-cards
            Two quiet minutes, then the maturity levels
            0:56–1:00 · 4 minutes
            1. Two minutes of quiet: stand up, roll your shoulders, breathe in for four counts and out for six. Nothing to do — on purpose.
            2. Then, in pairs, one minute each way: one partner says a number from 0 to 5; the other names the CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) maturity level and gives one sentence about it.
            0 Incomplete · 1 Initial · 2 Managed · 3 Defined · 4 Quantitatively Managed · 5 Optimizing.
